lead: An integrated optical waveguide traps light inside a narrow high-index strip or channel built on a chip. It uses total internal reflection, but confines light in two directions: vertically by the layer stack and horizontally by the strip edges. The core has index n1; substrate and cladding have lower index n2. Many optical functions then share one small chip, a photonic integrated circuit. Only a few universities teach this topic in detail. It is the geometry behind splitters, filters and Mach–Zehnder modulators (Unit 3).
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for modes in a planar layer and Chapter 1.6 for the single-mode cutoff idea.

blocks.text: An integrated waveguide is a dielectric layer stack on a chip. The core has refractive index n1. The substrate and cladding have refractive index n2, with n1 > n2. Light is guided when it strikes the core–cladding boundary above the critical angle, as in Chapter 1.2.

A planar guide confines light only in the vertical direction. Patterning the core into a strip adds horizontal confinement. A 3D guide is often called a channel waveguide; some syllabi use that name only for the buried rectangular core, and call the raised version a strip or ridge guide. The figure shows the layer order, not the width.

items: Raised strip or ridge: raised core; air or glass above; strong sidewall index step.
Buried channel: rectangular core inside cladding on all sides; smoother top surface.
Both need n1 > n2 at every boundary that guides the mode.

blocks.text: The substrate is the lower cladding. The upper cladding may be air or a deposited glass. In a channel guide the core is embedded, so top and sides see cladding.

Two index steps act together: vertical and horizontal. The field is not fully inside the core. Part travels as an evanescent tail in the cladding. The mode behaves as if it sees an effective index n_eff, with n2 < n_eff < n1. n_eff is the phase index of the guided mode.

blocks.where: V is the normalized frequency (dimensionless); t is core thickness in µm; λ is free-space wavelength in µm; n1 is core index; n2 is cladding or substrate index.

blocks.text: The numerical aperture is NA = √(n1² − n2²), dimensionless; here it measures the index step, not a launch angle in air.

A quick single-mode check in the thickness direction uses this V. For a symmetric slab stack, the thickness direction is approximately single-mode when V < π/2 ≈ 1.57. An asymmetric stack pushes the limit up towards π. The value V < 2.405 belongs to a step-index fibre (first zero of J0), not to this slab V. For a rectangular guide this is only an estimate because the width also matters.

Photonic integrated circuits place waveguides, splitters, gratings and modulators on one substrate. The same chip can route several wavelengths and modulate light. A Mach–Zehnder modulator splits a guided wave into two arms, changes phase in one arm and recombines the arms; see Unit 3, Optical modulators and Mach–Zehnder devices.
The width w also sets horizontal confinement. A guide can be single-mode vertically but multimode horizontally if w is large. Full design uses a mode solver. Go to Chapter 1.9 for periodic guides.

figure.caption: A strip waveguide cross-section: a high-index core strip lies between upper cladding and substrate. Light is confined vertically by these index steps and horizontally by the strip width.

spec.aria: A three-layer stack with a high-index core strip between upper cladding and substrate, showing vertical confinement.

examples.question: A strip waveguide has core thickness t = 0.5 µm, width w = 2 µm, n1 = 1.50, n2 = 1.45 and λ = 1.55 µm. Find NA and the approximate V for the thickness direction. State whether the thickness direction is approximately single-mode.
steps: Square the indices: n1² = 2.2500 and n2² = 2.1025.
Compare: 0.778 < 1.57, so the thickness direction is approximately single-mode. The width w = 2 µm is not checked by this formula.
examples.answer: NA ≈ 0.384, V ≈ 0.778, so the thickness direction is approximately single-mode because V < 1.57 (slab limit).
examples.check:
import math
n1 = 1.50
n2 = 1.45
t = 0.5
lam = 1.55
NA = math.sqrt(n1**2 - n2**2)
V = (2 * math.pi * t / lam) * NA
print(round(NA, 3))
print(round(V, 3))

traps: Terminology differs: some books call every 3D guide a channel waveguide; others reserve channel for a buried core and call the raised one a strip or ridge. Check which convention your paper uses.

Do not use the fibre cutoff V < 2.405 for a slab. For a symmetric stack the thickness direction is approximately single-mode when V < π/2 ≈ 1.57; asymmetric stacks approach π. For a rectangular guide even this is only an estimate.
Use consistent units for t and λ. The ratio t/λ is dimensionless; mixing µm and nm gives a wrong V.
Do not confuse effective index n_eff with core index n1. n_eff lies between n2 and n1.
A guide can be single-mode vertically and multimode horizontally. The width matters.

quiz.q: Define core, substrate and cladding indices.
quiz.a: Core n1 guides light; substrate and cladding have lower n2.

quiz.q: Why add a patterned strip to a planar guide?
quiz.a: Planar layers confine vertically; the strip adds horizontal index steps.

quiz.q: For t = 0.6 µm, λ = 1.3 µm, n1 = 1.48, n2 = 1.46, find approximate V.
V = 0.7 but width w = 8 µm: is the guide certainly single-mode?
quiz.a: No; V covers thickness only. A wide strip can support horizontal modes; use a 2D mode solver.
Phase index of the mode; n2 < n_eff < n1 because the field overlaps core and cladding.
Photonic integrated circuits, such as Mach–Zehnder modulator arms.

beyond: Not for the exam. Silicon photonics uses strip waveguides because silicon and silicon dioxide give a large index step, so bends can be sharp. Silicon nitride and lithium niobate platforms trade index step for lower loss or electro-optic modulation. Search next for 'silicon photonics waveguide', 'effective index method' and 'mode solver'.
